name: Hydrogen
blurb: The simplest and lightest element, a single proton paired with a single electron. Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, fueling stars through nuclear fusion.
uses: Rocket fuel when combined with liquid oxygen
facts: Makes up about 75% of the universe's normal matter
Burns with a nearly invisible pale blue flame
Was the gas that famously doomed the Hindenburg airship

name: Helium
appearance: colorless gas, exhibiting a red-orange glow when placed in a high-voltage electric field
blurb: A noble gas so unreactive it almost never forms compounds. Helium has the lowest boiling point of any element and stays liquid even near absolute zero.
uses: Deep-sea diving gas mixtures to prevent nitrogen narcosis
facts: First detected in the Sun's spectrum before being found on Earth
Second most abundant element in the universe after hydrogen
Makes voices sound high-pitched by changing the speed of sound

name: Lithium
blurb: The lightest metal and lightest solid element, soft enough to cut with a knife. Lithium reacts vigorously but not explosively with water.
facts: Floats on water and even on oil
Named after the Greek word for 'stone'
Central to the modern electric-vehicle battery industry

name: Beryllium
blurb: A hard, lightweight, steel-gray metal. Beryllium is prized for stiffness and low weight but its dust is highly toxic.
uses: Alloyed with copper for non-sparking tools
facts: Nearly transparent to X-rays
One of the stiffest metals by weight
Handling it requires strict safety controls due to toxicity

name: Boron
blurb: A hard, brittle metalloid that sits at the border between metals and nonmetals. Boron compounds are essential to plant growth.
facts: Extremely hard in its crystalline form
Essential micronutrient for plants
Boron-10 is used to absorb neutrons in nuclear reactors

name: Carbon
blurb: The backbone of all known life and organic chemistry. Carbon forms more compounds than any other element, from diamond to DNA.
uses: Graphite for pencils, lubricants, and electrodes
Diamond for cutting tools and jewelry
Activated carbon for water and air filtration
facts: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, just arranged differently
Radiocarbon (carbon-14) dating reveals the age of ancient artifacts
Carbon nanotubes are stronger than steel at a fraction of the weight

name: Nitrogen
blurb: A colorless, mostly inert diatomic gas that makes up most of Earth's atmosphere. Its triple bond makes N2 extremely stable.
uses: Fertilizer production via the Haber-Bosch process
Inert atmosphere for food packaging and electronics manufacturing
Liquid nitrogen for cryogenics and freezing
facts: Makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere by volume
Its triple bond is one of the strongest in chemistry
Liquid nitrogen boils at -196°C

name: Oxygen
blurb: A highly reactive gas essential for respiration and combustion. Oxygen readily forms compounds with almost every other element.
facts: Makes up about 21% of Earth's atmosphere
The ozone layer (O3) shields Earth from ultraviolet radiation
Third most abundant element in the universe

name: Fluorine
blurb: The most electronegative element and the most reactive nonmetal. Fluorine is so aggressive it can corrode glass and even react with some noble gases.
uses: Toothpaste and water fluoridation for cavity prevention
facts: Reacts with almost every other element, including some noble gases
Never found free in nature due to its extreme reactivity
Its compounds give Teflon its famously slippery surface

name: Neon
appearance: colorless gas exhibiting an orange-red glow when placed in a high voltage electric field
blurb: A noble gas that glows a distinctive reddish-orange when electrified, giving neon signs their name.
facts: Essentially chemically inert, forming no stable compounds
Named from the Greek word for 'new'
Present in Earth's atmosphere only in trace amounts

name: Sodium
blurb: A soft, silvery alkali metal that reacts violently with water, releasing hydrogen gas and heat.
uses: Table salt (sodium chloride) and food preservation
facts: Reactive enough to be stored under oil
Essential electrolyte for nerve and muscle function
Its name comes from 'natrium', the Latin name for soda

name: Magnesium
blurb: A lightweight, silvery metal that burns with a brilliant white flame. Magnesium is central to photosynthesis as the core of chlorophyll.
uses: Lightweight alloys for cars, laptops, and aircraft
facts: At the center of every chlorophyll molecule in plants
One of the lightest structural metals
Burns hot enough to ignite underwater fires

name: Aluminium
blurb: A lightweight, corrosion-resistant metal that is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust.
facts: Once more valuable than gold before cheap extraction methods existed
Naturally forms a thin protective oxide layer
Fully recyclable without losing quality

name: Silicon
blurb: A metalloid and the second most abundant element in Earth's crust. Silicon's ability to act as a semiconductor built the modern electronics industry.
facts: The 'Silicon' in Silicon Valley refers to this element's role in chips
Sand is mostly silicon dioxide
Second most abundant element in Earth's crust after oxygen

name: Phosphorus
appearance: colourless, waxy white, yellow, scarlet, red, violet, black
blurb: A reactive nonmetal that exists in several forms, including white phosphorus (which glows and ignites in air) and red phosphorus (more stable).
uses: Fertilizers (a key nutrient for plant growth)
DNA and ATP backbone in all living cells
facts: White phosphorus glows faintly in the dark, giving the element its name ('light-bearer')
Essential to DNA, RNA, and ATP in every living cell
Was first isolated from evaporated urine in 1669

name: Sulfur
blurb: A bright yellow nonmetal known for its distinctive smell in compounds like rotten eggs (hydrogen sulfide).
uses: Sulfuric acid production, the world's most-manufactured industrial chemical
facts: Often found as pure yellow crystals near volcanoes
Sulfuric acid made from it is the highest-volume industrial chemical worldwide
Responsible for the smell of rotten eggs and skunks (in compounds)

name: Chlorine
blurb: A pale green-yellow, toxic diatomic gas that is nonetheless essential for disinfecting water and producing table salt.
facts: Was used as a chemical weapon in World War I
Combines with sodium to form ordinary table salt
One of the most widely used industrial chemicals

name: Argon
appearance: colorless gas exhibiting a lilac/violet glow when placed in a high voltage electric field
blurb: The third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere, completely inert under normal conditions.
uses: Filling incandescent and fluorescent light bulbs
Preserving documents and wine from oxidation
facts: Makes up about 0.93% of Earth's atmosphere
Named from the Greek word for 'lazy' or 'inactive'
Forms essentially no stable chemical compounds

name: Potassium
blurb: A soft, highly reactive alkali metal essential to nerve function in the human body.
uses: Essential electrolyte in the human body (nerve and muscle function)
facts: Reacts violently with water, often bursting into lilac flame
Critical for regulating heartbeat and muscle contraction
Its symbol K comes from 'kalium', its Latin name

name: Calcium
blurb: An alkaline earth metal that is the most abundant metal in the human body, forming the mineral basis of bones and teeth.
facts: Makes up bones and teeth as calcium phosphate/carbonate
Fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust
Its compounds give limestone and marble their structure

name: Scandium
blurb: Scandium is a transition metal, part of the large central block of elements known for variable oxidation states and metallic bonding.
facts: Discovered by Lars Fredrik Nilson

name: Titanium

uses: White pigment (titanium dioxide) in paint and sunscreen
facts: As strong as steel but roughly 45% lighter
Biocompatible enough to fuse directly with human bone
Titanium dioxide is the most common white pigment on Earth

name: Vanadium
blurb: Vanadium is a transition metal, part of the large central block of elements known for variable oxidation states and metallic bonding.
facts: Discovered by Andrés Manuel del Río

name: Chromium
blurb: A hard, shiny transition metal that resists tarnishing, giving 'chrome' plating its brilliant mirror finish.
uses: Chrome plating for corrosion and wear resistance
facts: Named for the Greek word for 'color' due to its colorful compounds
Added to steel to make it stainless
Highly toxic in the hexavalent (Cr6+) form

name: Manganese
blurb: A brittle transition metal essential in steelmaking to remove impurities and add hardness.

Fertilizer and animal feed additive (essential trace nutrient)
facts: Nearly all steel produced today contains some manganese
Essential trace nutrient for humans, plants, and animals
Was one of the first metals used in prehistoric cave pigments

name: Iron
appearance: lustrous metallic with a grayish tinge

uses: Steel for construction, vehicles, and machinery
facts: Forms the core of the Earth, generating our magnetic field
Rusting is iron reacting slowly with oxygen and water
Most-produced metal by mass in the world

name: Cobalt

uses: Blue pigments in glass and ceramics (cobalt blue)
facts: Named after 'kobold', a mischievous mining spirit in German folklore
One of only three ferromagnetic elements at room temperature (with iron and nickel)
Vitamin B12 contains a cobalt atom at its core

name: Nickel
appearance: lustrous, metallic, and silver with a gold tinge
blurb: A silvery-white, corrosion-resistant transition metal alloyed into stainless steel and coins.
facts: One of only a few ferromagnetic elements

A key alloying element in stainless steel

facts: One of the few metals with a natural color other than gray or silver

Second-best electrical conductor among metals, after silver

name: Zinc

Fourth most widely used metal after iron, aluminum, and copper

name: Gallium

name: Germanium

name: Arsenic
